title: Agent Archivist control trust record envelope (archivist.control/v1)
description: The shared, versioned conventions every control trust record reuses (plan Section 5 control-plane boundary; docs/notes/control-trust-schemas.md). Control records are the tenant-authority-signed objects below `tenants/<tenant>/v1/control/` (plan Section 7.5): the linked-client, delegation, and key-rotation records shipped alongside this file, the revocation and receipt-key records beside them, and the authority-rotation record type the control-plane boundary names, arriving as its own schema composed from this document. This file is a conventions registry and shared member library, not an instance schema — the standing `ingest-identifiers.json` has in the wire family: no control object validates against it alone, and every record-type schema is the complete, closed, flat object (wrapper members from `wrapper.members` below plus the type's payload members, side by side, `additionalProperties: false`). The wrapper is deliberately not a nested envelope-with-record shape: the receipt-key certificate inside `ingest-receipt.json` is already a flat authority-signed control record, and the receipt-key record type consumes that definition — its payload members are the certificate's — rather than duplicating it (docs/notes/wire-schemas.md).

x-archivist.publicMaterialOnly: no member of any control record carries private-key material: every key-bearing member is a public half under a common shape, and the closed shape leaves no undeclared member for anything else to ride in (SEC-006). tools/check-control-schemas.py rejects private/secret/seed member names outright so the property is machine-checked, not aspirational
x-archivist.authorityChain: every control record is signed by the tenant authority: `authority_key_id` names the signing key and `authority_signature` carries the signature (construction `control-record-v1` below). In v1 the named key is the tenant authority root the client pinned during linking (ID-009); when the authority itself rotates, an authority-rotation record type chains successor keys to predecessor ones, and `authority_key_id` then names the signing authority record's key — the certificate's authority-resolution rule, applied family-wide. Verification always starts at the pinned root and walks forward; it never trusts a key because a record asserts it

writeClasses.immutable: written once at a record-type-derived key; the ControlAdminStore rejects an overwrite outright unless the bytes are the identical record (plan Section 5: it 'rejects overwrite of an incompatible immutable record'), so a lost-response retry of the same administrative write is an idempotent repair and nothing else can displace the object. No pointer is protected, so the signed epoch is not a wrapper requirement for this class — a type carries it only when the epoch is part of the record's identity (the revocation and rotation object keys name their epochs — the revoked epoch and the established epoch — and of the shipped immutable records those two are the ones that do; the receipt-key record's key names the certified key ID, not an epoch, so it carries no epoch member at all)
writeClasses.current-pointer: one object per subject at a fixed key, holding the current state; a replacement is accepted only when its signed `authorization_epoch` strictly increases — equal or lower is a stale write and is rejected (plan Section 5). The signature covers the epoch, so replaying an older record cannot displace a newer pointer without the authority key; rollback is therefore impossible by construction, the same property the plan pins for derived-policy pointers (publish another higher-epoch record, never repoint to an older one)

trustRecordCacheTtlSeconds.appliesTo: every control record an ingestion replica loads while authenticating an uploader — the linked-client record, a delegation record for relay attempts, a rotation record while an old-key overlap window is being served, a revocation record for the revoked-epoch check — and the receipt-key record a receipt signer loads to learn which certified key and window to sign under (all five shipped; authority-rotation records when they ship)
trustRecordCacheTtlSeconds.crossRef: schemas/v1/control-client.json, control-delegation.json, control-rotation.json, and control-receipt-key.json pin this value as x-archivist.trustRecordCacheTtlSeconds; schemas/v1/control-revocation.json pins it as x-archivist.revocationPropagationBoundSeconds; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves all six agree
trustRecordCacheTtlSeconds.description: The upper bound on how long a reader may serve a cached control record before re-reading the store (plan Section 5: trust records cache for at most 60 seconds; EC-09: a registry outage permits using an unexpired cached record for at most 60 seconds, then readiness comes off with a retryable 503 and no storage writes). Because a revocation takes effect through the reader's view of control state, this constant is also the maximum revocation propagation delay — the same number re-expressed where the revocation record needs it, never a second value.

authorizationWindowSeconds.appliesTo: the fresh-per-attempt authorization timestamp in the ingest attempt signature (schemas/v1/ingest-request.json)
authorizationWindowSeconds.crossRef: schemas/v1/ingest-request.json pins this value as x-archivist.authorizationWindowSeconds; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves the two agree
authorizationWindowSeconds.description: How long a fresh-per-attempt authorization proof stays valid (plan Section 5: request authorization is fresh per upload attempt and valid for five minutes; Section 7.2). A retry outside the window mints fresh authorization without changing occurrence or attestation identity, because attempt state never enters the immutable envelope. Registered here, beside the cache TTL, because the two bound the same exposure from opposite ends: revocation kills the epoch, this window kills the proof, and neither outlives its bound plus the skew allowance below.

clockSkewAllowanceSeconds.appliesTo: the age comparison at attempt verification: a timestamp within the authorization window is accepted with this much clock-skew tolerance in either direction
clockSkewAllowanceSeconds.crossRef: schemas/v1/ingest-request.json pins this value as x-archivist.clockSkewAllowanceSeconds; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves the two agree
clockSkewAllowanceSeconds.description: Clock-skew tolerance applied when checking the attempt timestamp against the authorization window (plan Section 5: valid for five minutes with at most five minutes of clock skew). Client and server clocks are not synchronized; the allowance keeps a legitimately fresh proof from failing on skew alone. It is named separately from the window rather than folded into it, because it protects a different clock — the verifier's, not the signer's — and the plan pins them as two five-minute values that must not silently become one ten-minute window.

rotationVerificationOverlapHours.appliesTo: the old/new-key verification overlap after a client key rotation: both the previous and the new public key verify for this long from the rotation record's signed_at (schemas/v1/control-rotation.json, which anchors the window, applies it)
rotationVerificationOverlapHours.crossRef: schemas/v1/control-client.json and schemas/v1/control-rotation.json pin this value as x-archivist.rotationVerificationOverlapHours; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves all three agree
rotationVerificationOverlapHours.description: How long both the previous and the new client key verify after a rotation (plan Section 5: 'Key rotation accepts old and new keys for 24 hours, and retries authorize the frozen envelope with the current key'). The overlap widens which key may sign, never which epoch is current — attempts present the current authorization epoch throughout — so a retry of an already-frozen envelope re-authorizes with fresh per-attempt state under either half instead of stranding in the spool (plan Phase 3 exit gate; EC-12), and after the window only the new key verifies. Registered in hours, not seconds, because the plan pins it as 24 hours and the constant mirrors the plan's number exactly; the unit field — not the name alone — carries the distinction from the second-valued constants beside it.

receiptKeyRotationDays.appliesTo: the receipt-key signing-window cadence: how often the tenant authority certifies a fresh receipt key (schemas/v1/control-receipt-key.json, the authoritative control-prefix record; the certificate embedded by value in every receipt, schemas/v1/ingest-receipt.json)
receiptKeyRotationDays.crossRef: schemas/v1/control-receipt-key.json and the certificate definition in schemas/v1/ingest-receipt.json pin this value as x-archivist.receiptKeyRotationDays; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves all three agree
receiptKeyRotationDays.description: How often a fresh server receipt key is certified (plan Section 7.8: 'Receipt keys rotate every 30 days with seven days of old/new signing overlap'). Successor signing windows open every 30 days and each key signs for the rotation plus the overlap — 37 days — so the cadence is what keeps exactly one fresh certification per month while the overlap constant below keeps the boundary covered. Rotation is non-invalidating by the record's write class, not by this number: the receipt-key record is immutable and key-addressed, so certifying a fresh key writes a new object and every retained certificate keeps verifying indefinitely (ID-009). Registered in days, not seconds, because the plan pins it as 30 days and the constant mirrors the plan's number exactly.

receiptKeySigningOverlapDays.appliesTo: the receipt-key signing-window overlap: how long each certified key keeps signing past its successor's first signing instant (schemas/v1/control-receipt-key.json; the certificate in schemas/v1/ingest-receipt.json)
receiptKeySigningOverlapDays.crossRef: schemas/v1/control-receipt-key.json and the certificate definition in schemas/v1/ingest-receipt.json pin this value as x-archivist.receiptKeySigningOverlapDays; tools/check-control-schemas.py proves all three agree
receiptKeySigningOverlapDays.description: The old/new signing overlap on receipt keys (plan Section 7.8): each key signs for seven days past its successor's start, so a replacement begins signing before its predecessor stops and the signer is never without a valid key across a rotation boundary — including one that lands late, since a successor certified inside the last seven days of its predecessor's window still leaves both valid. It bounds signing only, never verification: an expired key's receipts verify for as long as their certificates are retained, which immutability makes forever (ID-009). Named separately from the rotation constant because it serves a different guarantee — signing continuity across the boundary, not the cadence — and the two sum to the window length a reader can check from any single record (`valid_until` − `valid_from`, VAL-002).

signatures.key: the tenant authority key named by `authority_key_id` — the pinned root in v1, or an authority record's key once authority rotation exists (ID-009)
covered: canonical record bytes minus the `authority_signature` member
signatures.description: Ed25519 over the RFC 8785 canonicalization of the complete record object with the `authority_signature` member removed — exactly the receipt-key-v1 shape (schemas/v1/ingest-identifiers.json), reused deliberately so one verifier core walks both families. Domain separation under one authority key comes from the member sets: every control record's signed bytes contain the `schema` namespace member and no bare certificate's do, so the two signed byte ranges stay structurally distinct.

recordTypes.description: The linked-client record (plan Section 7.5 `tenants/<tenant>/v1/control/clients/<client>.json`): client identity, Ed25519 public key, base scopes, and the current authorization epoch (ID-003).

The revocation record (plan Section 7.5 `tenants/<tenant>/v1/control/revocations/<client>/<epoch>.json`): the append-only, epoch-addressed revocation of one client's authorization at one epoch (plan Section 5; ID-006), written together with a strictly higher-epoch linked-client pointer that is what actually fails stale-epoch attempts closed. `keyMembers` names the members the store derives the object key from — for this type the epoch is identity, not a pointer guard.

The delegation record (plan Section 5: origin/uploader delegation for approved relays; ID-005): the relay grant — one uploader client authorized to present one origin client's frozen occurrences. Relay authority is the conjunction of tenant, origin, harness, and operation scopes, never their union (plan Section 5), and the shape enforces it: one current object per (relay, origin) pair, an explicit harness and operation allowlist intersected with the relay's own, and a closed state member whose `withdrawn` value is the only withdrawal a current-pointer shape permits.

The key-rotation record (plan Section 5: key rotation accepts old and new keys for 24 hours; Phase 3: overlapping verification with monotonic authorization epochs): the durable evidence of one client key rotation — the epoch it establishes, the previous epoch, both public halves, and the 24-hour overlap during which both verify so retries of a frozen envelope authorize under either key, read by stateless replicas from this record rather than server-local state. `keyMembers` names the members the store derives the object key from — the established epoch is identity, exactly like the revocation's revoked epoch.

The receipt-key record (plan Section 7.5 `tenants/<tenant>/v1/control/receipt-keys/<key>.json`; Section 7.8): the tenant-authority certification of one server receipt-signing key — the public half, its pinned derivation, the algorithm, and the signing window — as the authoritative control-prefix source of the receipt-key certificate embedded by value in every receipt the key signs (schemas/v1/ingest-receipt.json), whose members are this record's payload members. One immutable object per key ID: rotation certifies a fresh key as a fresh object and never rewrites a predecessor, so retained receipts keep verifying indefinitely (ID-009). Key-addressed, not epoch-addressed — the one shipped immutable type that carries no `authorization_epoch`, because its identity is the certified key ID its key names.

schema-namespace.description: The control trust namespace, expressed the way the `archivist.error/v1` and `archivist.cli-output/v1` families express theirs: one namespace member, present in every record, never implied by context, so a reader knows which contract it is reading before it looks at anything else. The trailing `v1` is the family's only version axis — there is no numeric twin beside it, and a v2 is a new namespace string, never a second field. Security-bearing: an unknown namespace fails closed; a trust record a reader cannot interpret is a verification failure, never a best-effort parse.

record-type.description: Which control record type the object is (plan Section 5: client, delegation, rotation, revocation, and receipt-verification-key records all live under the control prefix). Closed, and appended to only by the change that ships the new type's schema and its readers: v1 ships `linked-client`, `revocation`, `delegation`, `rotation`, and `receipt-key`; the authority-rotation token arrives with its record type and old readers fail closed on it until upgraded — the plan Section 7.1 rule that unknown security-bearing values are never guessed. Each record-type schema pins this member to a const of its own token, so a record of one type can never validate as the other. Security-bearing.

record-kind.description: The write class (plan Section 5): `immutable` records are written once at a derived key with incompatible overwrites rejected; `current-pointer` records hold the current state of one subject and a replacement is valid only when its signed epoch increases (see `writeClasses`). The member must equal the write class registered for `record_type` in this schema's `recordTypes` registry — a cross-field check the ControlAdminStore makes before any write and any reader can re-make (VAL-002-style, not schema syntax). Security-bearing: the write rule is an authorization decision, so an unknown value fails closed.

authorization-epoch.description: The signed monotonic authorization epoch (plan Section 5: a current-pointer replacement is permitted only when its signed epoch increases; plan Phase 3: monotonic authorization epochs). Required on every current-pointer record; an immutable record type carries it only when the epoch is part of its identity (the revocation and rotation object keys name their epochs — the revoked and the established — and the shipped records of both types require it as the identity member that equals that key segment). The authority signature covers it, so a stale record cannot displace a newer pointer and a revocation or rotation cannot be re-dated. Monotonic per subject — a client for the client-family records, the (relay, origin) relation for a delegation record: every current-pointer's epoch only increases, each revocation permanently fixes the epoch it revokes, and each rotation permanently fixes the epoch it establishes, so every subject's authorization history is a strictly ascending sequence that no later write reorders — which is why revocation and rotation can be append-only. The maximum is the 18-digit canonical decimal the revocation object key can carry — the bound is held in lockstep with that grammar rather than at the raw u63 ceiling, and sits far above any real epoch count. On the wire, an attempt's authorization epoch must equal the current linked-client record's epoch: stale-epoch attempts fail closed (plan Phase 3 exit gate), and the receipt records which epoch actually authorized the commit.

client-object-key.description: Server-derived linked-client record key (plan Section 7.5): tenant, the fixed v1 control prefix, and the validated client UUID. One object per linked client — the current-pointer home whose replacement requires a strictly higher signed epoch. The tenant segment must equal the record's `tenant_id` and the client segment its `client_id` (VAL-002 cross-field checks at the store and at any reader; ID-008: keys are derived from validated fields, never chosen by a writer).

revocation-object-key.description: Server-derived revocation record key (plan Section 7.5): tenant, the revoked client, and the revoked authorization epoch in canonical decimal without leading zeros. One immutable object per (client, epoch) — the epoch addressing that makes revocation append-only, since a new revocation can only be a new epoch and no write ever removes or rewrites an old one. The tenant segment must equal the record's `tenant_id`, the client segment its `client_id`, and the epoch segment its signed `authorization_epoch` (VAL-002 cross-field checks at the store and at any reader; ID-008: keys are derived from validated fields, never chosen by a writer). The epoch grammar `[1-9][0-9]{0,17}` and the `authorization-epoch` maximum are held in lockstep — 18 decimal digits at the ceiling — and the gate proves it on the boundary value.

delegation-object-key.description: Server-derived delegation record key: tenant, the relay (uploader) client, and the origin client — one current-pointer object per (relay, origin) pair, the exact pair a relay grant is the conjunction over. There is one object per pair and never one per client or per grant, so no reader can union grants: the current state of a relay's authority for one origin is always this one object. The tenant segment must equal the record's `tenant_id`, the first client segment its `relay_client_id`, and the second its `origin_client_id` (VAL-002 cross-field checks at the store and at any reader; ID-008). The two client segments are structurally indistinguishable to the pattern — the store's segment-equality checks are what keep a swapped key from being read as the reverse grant, and `relay_client_id` must never equal `origin_client_id` (self-delegation is rejected as a cross-field check, not schema syntax).

rotation-object-key.description: Server-derived key-rotation record key: tenant, the rotating client, and the authorization epoch the rotation establishes, in canonical decimal without leading zeros. One immutable object per (client, established epoch) — the epoch addressing that makes the rotation history append-only, addressed by the epoch it establishes so a reader holding the linked-client pointer at epoch E finds the overlap evidence for E's key at exactly `rotations/<client>/E.json`. The tenant segment must equal the record's `tenant_id`, the client segment its `client_id`, and the epoch segment its signed `authorization_epoch` (VAL-002 cross-field checks at the store and at any reader; ID-008). The epoch grammar `[1-9][0-9]{0,17}` and the `authorization-epoch` maximum are held in lockstep — 18 decimal digits at the ceiling — the same lockstep the revocation key's grammar keeps, and the gate proves it on the boundary value for both.

receipt-key-object-key.description: Server-derived receipt-key record key (plan Section 7.5): tenant and the receipt key ID — the lowercase-hex SHA-256 of the encoded public key, so the key segment is computable from the record's own `public_key` under the pinned derivation. One immutable object per key ID: rotation certifies a fresh key as a fresh object and never rewrites a predecessor, which is what keeps every retained receipt's certificate in the store and verifying (ID-009). The tenant segment must equal the record's `tenant_id` and the key segment its `key_id` (VAL-002 cross-field checks at the store and at any reader; ID-008). Must stay in agreement with the receipt-key certificate's documented `objectKey` in `schemas/v1/ingest-receipt.json` — the certificate definition is what the receipt-key record type consumes, not duplicates; tools/check-control-schemas.py cross-checks the two and proves the member-for-member agreement.
